transcript.text: My Dyson V10 Absolute (SV12) won't run at all now. On the battery display there's a red light flashing when I press the trigger, then nothing. It was charging overnight. Do I need a new battery or is the whole thing dead?

It is not automatically proof that the whole vacuum is dead. A V10 that flashes red at the trigger and will not start is most often a battery/charging issue, but a blocked airway or filter can also make its protection cut in. The charger or its contacts are the other sensible possibility before blaming the vacuum itself. I cannot confirm the flashing red light as a specific error code for this model from that description, so I would work from the symptoms rather than treat it as a definite code. 1. Try the charger in a known-working wall socket and make sure its plug is fully home in the vacuum or dock. With the charger unplugged first, wipe the charging contacts with a dry cloth, then reconnect it. Check whether any charging light appears. No charging indication points more towards the charger, its connection, or the battery. 2. With the vacuum switched off, empty the bin and remove the wand and floorhead. Look through the wand, bin inlet and floorhead for a blockage; also check the brush bar turns freely. A blockage can trigger protection, although it more commonly causes pulsing or brief running rather than no start at all. 3. Check the filters are clean and completely dry. If they need washing, use cold water only and leave them to dry for at least 24 hours before refitting; a damp filter can cause problems. If it still only flashes red after the charging and airflow checks, the battery becomes the leading suspect, rather than the complete machine. An internal motor or control fault is possible but less likely at this stage.

Tried a different socket and the charger light is on. Blue lights come on while charging, but it still just flashes red when I press the trigger. Filter was washed last month and the bin and airways are clear, nothing blocked. Battery isn't swollen, hot or smelly.

The leading suspect is now the battery: it can show blue charging lights yet fail as soon as the motor demands power. The next possibility is a fault in the main body’s motor/control electronics. 1. With the vacuum switched off, remove the wand and floorhead. Press the trigger with only the handheld body attached. - If it still immediately flashes red and does not run, that strongly supports a failing battery pack, though an engineer would need to rule out the main-body electronics before replacing anything. - If it runs normally as a handheld, the issue is in the wand or motorised floorhead rather than the battery. Do not keep repeatedly pulling the trigger if the red warning continues.

I'm not sure what it does with just the handheld body, I haven't tried it that way. It does the same flashing red with everything attached, though. I haven't got a spare V10 battery to swap in, and I won't unscrew anything in case Dyson want to look at it.

You do not need to unscrew or dismantle anything for the useful next test. The blue charge lights show it is accepting charge, but they do not prove the battery can deliver power to the motor. With the clear airways and no battery swelling, the battery pack is still the most likely fault; the main-body motor/control electronics are the alternative. 1. With the vacuum off, release the wand and floorhead in the normal way—no tools or screws.
2. Leave the bin and filter in place, then press the trigger once briefly. If it still flashes red immediately with just the handheld body, that makes a battery-pack fault more likely than a floorhead or wand fault. It would not prove it absolutely, as the main body electronics can produce a similar result, but it is the best non-invasive separator. If it runs without the wand, the fault is instead in the wand or motorised floorhead. If you prefer not to do even that test, stop using/charging it unnecessarily and arrange Dyson support or a vacuum repair engineer; they can test the battery and main body without you dismantling it.

candidates: Battery not accepting or delivering charge (high)
Charger, socket or dirty charging contacts (medium)
Internal motor or control electronics fault (low)

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.

Explain what the error code means using ERROR CODES. If ERROR CODES does not resolve it, say plainly that you cannot confirm what it means on their model (it may not be an error code at all, for example part of the model name), never guess a meaning, and work from the symptoms.

claimsRejected.claim: There is no sign from what you have found that the whole vacuum is definitely dead; the battery is the most likely replaceable item at this point, but this attachment-free test is the useful confirmation before spending money.
